Volume 06 · Chapter 08

Business cycles and stabilization models

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v06-c07

By the endCompare short-run models and identify their assumptions and predictions.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can close a short-run macroeconomic model, solve its equilibrium under a stated policy instrument, distinguish price-level adjustment from inflation dynamics, and compare real and nominal explanations of fluctuations. You can identify when a rate floor changes the solution and explain why a conditional model prediction is not an identified empirical effect.

Read Inflation, expectations and nominal rigidity, retaining the banking distinctions in Chapter 6 and the dated household and investment budgets in Chapter 4. We use linear systems, constrained optimization and conditional expectations. Every numerical economy below is original and synthetic. Equations are maintained assumptions or derived implications, not estimates from observed national data.

1. A model needs an instrument, an information date and a closure

A business-cycle fluctuation is movement in aggregate activity around a specified reference path. That description does not identify a cause. A shock changes a primitive or an exogenous input relative to a baseline; an equilibrium response is the joint change in variables satisfying all the model's equations. A policy rule responding to activity is not the same object as an unexpected change in that rule.

A model is closed when it specifies enough behavioral relationships, resource and market-clearing conditions, policy choices and boundary conditions to determine its endogenous variables. Counting equations is useful but insufficient: equations may be dependent, have several roots or imply infeasible quantities. We prove uniqueness only for the particular systems below. A model with predetermined prices, a flexible-price real economy and a forward-looking price-setting economy are separate experiments. Their parameters and equilibria cannot be spliced together without a new argument.

Fix one period length throughout each experiment. Let Pₜ > 0 be a price index. Ordinary net inflation is πₜg = Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁ − 1; log inflation in log points is Πₜ = 100 ln(Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁). For a nominal net interest rate iₜg > −1, define the nominal log rate ιₜ = 100 ln(1 + iₜg). The realized real gross return on a nominal claim held from t to t + 1 is

1 + rₜg = (1 + iₜg)/(Pₜ₊₁/Pₜ),
so 100 ln(1 + rₜg) = ιₜ − Πₜ₊₁.

When the nominal rate is known at t, its expected log real return is ιₜ − EₜΠₜ₊₁, where Eₜ means a conditional expectation using date-t information. This is not generally the expected ordinary net real return. The logarithmic identity is exact; the behavioral linear equations used later are approximations or explicit reduced-form assumptions. A log rate of 3 means an ordinary nominal rate exp(0.03) − 1, about 3.0455%, not exactly 3%. Small log points are approximately ordinary percentage points, but we retain their stated units.

2. IS–LM: goods and money markets under a fixed price level

Consider a closed economy with a fixed current P and available productive capacity. Output Y, consumption C, investment I, government consumption G and lump-sum taxes T are real goods per period. There is no government investment in this experiment; I covers all its capital formation. Firms meet planned spending within the stated capacity domain. Set

C = c₀ + c(Y − T),   0 < c < 1,
I = I₀ − b(ι − e + z),   b > 0,
Y = C + I + G,
m = M/P = kY − hι,   k,h > 0.

c is the marginal propensity to consume disposable income. I₀ is autonomous planned investment. e is expected next-period log inflation, held fixed in this experiment; z ≥ 0 is an extra borrowing premium in log-rate points. Thus investment responds to its expected real financing cost ι − e + z. This single premium summarizes a channel; it is not a bank balance-sheet model. M is a nominal money stock, m its real purchasing power, and kY − hι is real money demand. k has units of real balances per output flow and h balances per rate point. Money's opportunity cost is nominal, whereas this investment schedule uses an expected real rate. b is investment goods per rate point.

The IS relationship consists of output–rate combinations clearing the goods market. Write g = 1 − c and a = c₀ − cT + I₀ + G + be − bz. Substitution gives gY + bι = a. The LM relationship clears money holdings at the chosen supply m. It is a portfolio-demand condition, not a statement that each extra reserve mechanically produces a fixed multiple of loans. We assume this simplified money market and interest-sensitive investment; the previous banking chapter explains why they are not a complete description of monetary implementation.

ι = (kY − m)/h,
D = g + bk/h > 0,
Y = [a + (b/h)m]/D,   ι = (kY − m)/h.

Substituting the second market into the first leaves a scalar equation with positive coefficient D, proving a unique algebraic solution. Admissibility is a separate check: Y must lie within productive capacity, disposable income and planned quantities must satisfy their maintained domains, and any rate restriction must hold. If the solution violates them, this linear model has no admissible equilibrium for that experiment; clipping a quantity does not preserve both equations.

Comparative statics and the instrument choice

Holding the coefficients, P, other inputs and active domains fixed, differentiation gives

∂Y/∂G = 1/D,   ∂Y/∂T = −c/D,
∂Y/∂m = b/(hD),   ∂Y/∂e = b/D,   ∂Y/∂z = −b/D.

At fixed m, ∂ι/∂G = k/(hD): spending raises money demand and the rate, partly reducing investment. This is the model's crowding-out channel. It does not say public spending can never raise productive capacity, because that channel is absent here. Also ∂ι/∂m = −g/(hD), obtained by differentiating both terms in ι. Higher money supply lowers the rate and raises investment within this closure.

If the authority instead pegs ι at a chosen ῑ and supplies the required money, the solution is Y = (a − bῑ)/g and m = kY − hῑ. Now ∂Y/∂G = 1/g. The money quantity is endogenous; it cannot simultaneously be independently fixed unless the two targets happen to coincide. The required m must remain nonnegative and operationally available. A rate rule that changes ι with activity is a third closure, developed below. Caballero's inspected MIT lecture provides the goods-market and money-demand method and distinguishes a chosen rate from a chosen money quantity. Our linear schedules and comparisons are separately derived.

Worked example 1 — The same budget change under two monetary instruments

Let C = 20 + (3/5)(Y − T), I = 30 − 2(ι − e + z), T = G = 20, e = z = 0 and m = Y/2 − 5ι. Maintain 20 ≤ Y ≤ 200, 0 ≤ ι ≤ 15 and nonnegative C, I and money demand. With m = 50, IS is (2/5)Y + 2ι = 58. Since D = 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5, Y = 130 and ι = 3. Then C = 86, I = 24 and 86 + 24 + 20 = 130; money demand is 65 − 15 = 50.

Raise G to 26, financing its extra 6 with current government borrowing while T stays 20. At fixed m, Y rises by 6/(3/5) = 10 to 140; ι rises to 4, C to 92 and I falls to 22. Resources reconcile as 140 = 92 + 22 + 26. This one-period spending closure omits later debt service and future-tax effects on current consumption; it is not a lifetime welfare or fiscal-solvency calculation.

If instead the authority holds ι = 3, Y = (64 − 6)/(2/5) = 145, C = 95 and I = 24. Required money is m = 145/2 − 15 = 115/2 = 57.5. The larger response reflects a different instrument and accommodation of money demand. Both solutions satisfy the stated domains. Saying simply “the multiplier is 2.5” would leave out the condition that the nominal rate and expected inflation are held fixed.

3. From an IS–LM solution to a price-level AD–AS model

Aggregate demand here is the equilibrium Y at each possible current price P, holding nominal M, expected inflation e and the other inputs fixed. It is not just the consumption schedule. From the solution above,

YAD(P) = [a + (b/h)M/P]/D,   P > 0.
dYAD/dP = −bM/(hDP²) < 0 when M > 0.

A higher P reduces real balances and, through this particular money instrument, reduces activity. Under a fixed nominal-rate peg with unchanged e, this channel disappears. AD's slope therefore depends on the policy closure.

For a bounded short-run supply experiment, posit P = Pᵉ + ν(Y − Ȳ) + s, ν > 0. Pᵉ is a predetermined reference price, Ȳ a fixed reference output and s a supply-cost shift measured in price-index units. This is a price-level supply equation, not the forward inflation equation used later. It summarizes rising marginal costs with output while some nominal costs are preset; we do not claim to derive it from a fully specified wage bargain. In inverse form, supply output increases strictly with P while demand output decreases. Hence there is at most one positive-price intersection; existence and the quantitative domains still need checking.

Worked example 2 — An identical price increase can conceal different disturbances

Use the baseline goods equations with M = 100 and supply P = 2 + (Y − 130)/50 + s. At s = 0, P = 2 gives m = 50 and Y = 130. Demand is Y = 290/3 + 200/(3P); inverse supply is Y = 50P + 30.

First raise G by 6, with T fixed as before. Demand becomes Y = 320/3 + 200/(3P). Equating it with 50P + 30 gives 15P² − 23P − 20 = 0. Only one root is positive:

P* = (23 + √1729)/30 ≈ 2.152708,
Y* = 50P* + 30 ≈ 137.635410.

The other root is negative and outside P > 0. The rate is ι = (64 − (2/5)Y*)/2 ≈ 4.472918, within its domain; C and I remain positive. Price adjustment reduces the output increase below the fixed-price increase of 10.

Separately restore G = 20 and raise the supply shift to s = 1/5. Now inverse supply is Y = 50P + 20. Equating baseline demand to it produces the same quadratic. Thus P is unchanged from the first experiment, but Y = 50P* + 20 ≈ 127.635410 and ι ≈ 3.472918. Money demand still equals 100/P*, and both goods ledgers clear. The adverse supply shift raises the price while reducing output; the demand shift raises both.

If the preceding price was 2, either experiment produces log inflation 100 ln(P*/2) ≈ 7.357949 points during this adjustment. If the price stays at P* thereafter, the following period's inflation is zero. A one-time level increase is not a proof of continuing inflation. Observing only the current price change cannot distinguish these two disturbances; output helps within this model, but unobserved policy and simultaneous shocks can still confound an empirical comparison.

4. A finite real-business-cycle benchmark

Real business cycle reasoning studies how technology, preferences and other real changes alter feasible production and intertemporal choices in a market-clearing economy. A full model often chooses labor as well as consumption and capital. We isolate one channel in a two-date competitive, frictionless one-good benchmark: labor is fixed at one, initial physical capital K₀ = 1 is predetermined, production is Yₜ = Aₜ√Kₜ with Aₜ > 0, and capital fully depreciates after each date's production. One unit of current investment creates one unit of next-date capital. There is no government, trade, uncertainty, installation cost or financial wedge.

C₀ + I₀ = Y₀ = A₀,   K₁ = I₀,
C₁ = Y₁ = A₁√I₀,   0 < I₀ < Y₀.
Choose I₀ to maximize F(I₀) = ln(Y₀ − I₀) + βR ln(A₁√I₀),   βR > 0.

βR is the weight on terminal utility in this separate real model. At date 1 there is no later production or bequest: all output is consumed, with no terminal investment. These resource and terminal conditions prevent us from treating investment as an unfinanced addition to consumption. Both consumption levels must be positive before taking logarithms.

F′(I₀) = −1/(Y₀ − I₀) + βR/(2I₀),
F″(I₀) = −1/(Y₀ − I₀)² − βR/(2I₀²) < 0,
I₀* = βRY₀/(2 + βR),   C₀* = 2Y₀/(2 + βR).

The objective tends to minus infinity at either endpoint. Its interior stationary point exists, is feasible and is the unique global optimum by strict concavity. Equivalently, the Euler equation equates 1/C₀ with βR(A₁/(2√I₀))/C₁. The marginal product is the real return to investment in this full-depreciation case; the marginal utility of terminal consumption matters as well. Wolf's inspected real-business-cycle notes set out resource constraints, factor returns, household conditions and boundary requirements. This finite fixed-labor example is deliberately narrower.

Worked example 3 — Current technology and anticipated future technology

With Y₀ = A₀ = 12, A₁ = 6 and βR = 1, choose I₀ = 4, C₀ = 8 and C₁ = 12. The marginal product at date 1 is 6/(2√4) = 3/2; multiplying by terminal marginal utility 1/12 gives 1/8, matching current marginal utility.

A current productivity increase to A₀ = 15, holding A₁ fixed, gives I₀ = 5, C₀ = 10 and C₁ = 6√5. More current resources raise both consumption and investment. In contrast, announcing A₁ = 9 with current Y₀ still 12 leaves I₀ = 4 and C₀ = 8, while C₁ rises to 18. The larger marginal product exactly offsets the lower marginal utility of future consumption. Algebraically, βR ln A₁ is an additive constant in F(I₀). This cancellation depends on log utility, multiplicative technology and the other restrictions; anticipated productivity need not leave investment unchanged in a more general model.

No nominal variable enters this feasible set or objective. Changing only the unit in which all prices are quoted cannot alter this allocation. That conditional neutrality result does not show that monetary policy is ineffective with sticky prices, debt constraints or other omitted frictions. Nor does a fall in technology imply a gap below unchanged “potential”: feasible or flexible-price output can itself move.

5. A forward-looking New Keynesian system with an explicit ending

A small New Keynesian model combines intertemporal demand with nominal rigidity and an interest-rate policy. We take the following linearized three-equation system as a maintained reduced model; we do not derive a full price-setting contract or calibrate all its coefficients from a common optimizing economy. Galí's inspected lecture gives the forward dynamic-demand, inflation and policy structure. Its infinite-horizon extensions are not required here.

Let Yₜⁿ > 0 be the model's flexible-price output under the same real shocks, and xₜ = 100 ln(Yₜ/Yₜⁿ) its output gap in log points. A gap against an unchanged statistical trend is different. Πₜ is total log inflation as defined earlier, with a zero inflation target in this experiment. The steady nominal and real log rate is 2. Define jₜ = ιₜ − 2, the nominal-rate deviation, and nₜ = rₜⁿ − 2, the deviation of the natural real log rate. The natural rate rₜⁿ is the real rate consistent with the flexible-price benchmark's intertemporal demand. Its path is supplied, not estimated from the observed policy rate.

Dynamic demand: xₜ = Eₜxₜ₊₁ − σ(jₜ − EₜΠₜ₊₁ − nₜ),   σ > 0.
Inflation: Πₜ = βPEₜΠₜ₊₁ + κxₜ + uₜ,   0 ≤ βP ≤ 1, κ > 0.
Policy: jₜ = max{jmin, φπΠₜ + φxxₜ + vₜ},   φπ,φx ≥ 0.

σ is the demand sensitivity to an expected real-rate gap, κ the inflation slope, βP a supplied forward coefficient, uₜ a cost-push wedge in inflation points, and vₜ an exogenous policy disturbance in rate points. βP is not identified with βR from our separate real model or used to infer this model's steady real rate. All coefficients are for the same period length. The numerical floor is jmin = −2: since ιₜ = 2 + jₜ, it imposes a zero nominal log rate, equivalent to a zero ordinary nominal net rate. This is an assumed policy constraint, not a claim that negative rates are impossible in every monetary system.

The demand equation expresses a substitution channel: a higher expected real rate relative to the natural rate lowers current relative spending. Its gap form subtracts a flexible-price demand equation from the sticky-price one; the reference path and natural rate must use the same primitives. Supply says current inflation depends on expected future inflation, the gap and a wedge. In Chapter 7's preset-price example, the relevant forecast was Eₜ₋₁Πₜ and the illustrated target was 2. Here the forecast is EₜΠₜ₊₁ and the target is zero. Neither the date nor the normalization carries over silently. A cost wedge u is not automatically identical to a productivity shock: productivity can also change Yⁿ and n.

Finite closure and a uniqueness proof

Our lab has dates 0,…,T and supplies terminal values xT+1 and ΠT+1. Announced shock paths are deterministic and known at date 0, so conditional forecasts equal the next values on the solved path. The terminal values represent an externally specified continuation, not a theorem that a temporary shock must disappear at the horizon. A surprise learned later has a different earlier information set. We solve the announced case backward; a stochastic extension would need conditional distributions at every future node.

At one date, given X = Eₜxₜ₊₁ and E = EₜΠₜ₊₁, let B = βPE + uₜ. First ignore the floor. Substitution of inflation and policy into demand yields

DN = 1 + σ(φπκ + φx) > 0,
xᵘ = [X + σ(E + nₜ − vₜ − φπB)]/DN,
Πᵘ = B + κxᵘ,   jᵘ = φπΠᵘ + φxxᵘ + vₜ.

If jᵘ ≥ jmin, this solution is admissible. Otherwise set the actual rate to the floor and recompute both other variables:

j = jmin,   x = X + σ(E + nₜ − jmin),   Π = B + κx.
Check φπΠ + φxx + vₜ ≤ jmin.

Why does this give the unique branch? Write H = X + σ(E + nₜ), so demand gives x = H − σj. The unconstrained requested rate becomes K − σAj, where A = φπκ + φx ≥ 0 and K = φπB + AH + vₜ. The equilibrium equation is j = max{jmin, K − σAj}. Its left side strictly increases and right side weakly decreases. The unconstrained root is K/(1 + σA). If it lies below the floor, K < (1 + σA)jmin, which implies the floor's requested rate is below the floor; thus that branch satisfies the inequality. At equality both formulas give the same allocation. Every date has one finite solution, so backward induction gives a unique finite path for finite inputs and a supplied finite terminal condition.

This proof uses no restriction φπ > 1. Infinite-horizon rational-expectations determinacy is a different question: a finite terminal condition cannot be discarded while keeping this argument. Likewise, mathematical uniqueness does not make a large-gap linear approximation quantitatively accurate. The lab bounds its input and horizon sizes for a small, reproducible exercise; there is no claim of uniform bounds or stability as the horizon tends to infinity.

Worked example 4 — Demand, costs, news and the floor

Set σ = 1, βP = κ = 1/2, φπ = 2, φx = 0, jmin = −2 and terminal forecasts X = E = 0. Then DN = 2. For a demand disturbance n = −2 with u = v = 0, the solution is x = −1, Π = −1/2 and j = −1: total nominal ι is 1. For a cost disturbance u = 1 with n = v = 0, instead x = −1, Π = 1/2 and j = 1. Equal negative output gaps coexist with opposite inflation and rate movements.

For n = −6 and u = v = 0, ignoring the floor gives xᵘ = −3, Πᵘ = −3/2 and jᵘ = −3, which is infeasible. Recompute at j = −2: x = −4, Π = −2 and requested rate 2Π = −4 ≤ −2. Keeping x = −3 while merely replacing j by −2 would violate demand. These are substantial model gaps; use them to understand a boundary, not as a measured forecast.

Now take dates 0 and 1, terminal x₂ = Π₂ = 0, and announce at date 0 that only n₁ = −2. At date 1 the first solution applies. At date 0, X = −1, E = −1/2 and n₀ = u₀ = v₀ = 0. The formula gives x₀ = −1/2, Π₀ = −1/2 and j₀ = −1. Directly, demand is −1 − [−1 − (−1/2)] = −1/2 and supply is (1/2)(−1/2) + (1/2)(−1/2) = −1/2. Anticipated future weakness affects current outcomes. If date-0 agents instead forecast the zero-shock baseline and learn of an unforeseen disturbance only at date 1, their date-0 solution would be zero and their date-1 plan would then change. That compares specified information histories; it does not supply a common stochastic rational-expectations model in which a zero-probability event nevertheless occurs. Under ordinary uncertain news, one must supply the earlier probability distribution, not label an already known shock a surprise.

6. Stabilization objectives and what the models leave open

A policy rule is not automatically an optimal policy. To make “better stabilization” meaningful, specify an objective and feasible instruments. For a one-date problem with zero next-date forecasts, let the authority choose j ≥ −2 to minimize L = Π² + ωx², with ω > 0, subject to demand x = n − j and supply Π = κx + u (σ = 1). This loss is measured in squared log points. It is a stated criterion; it is not an empirically estimated social welfare function. Wolf's inspected monetary-policy notes motivate the constrained inflation–activity tradeoff; our weights and floor case are original.

L(x) = (κ² + ω)x² + 2κux + u²,
xᵘ = −κu/(κ² + ω),   Πᵘ = ωu/(κ² + ω),
x ≤ n + 2 from the rate floor, hence x* = min{xᵘ, n + 2},   j* = n − x*.

Completing the square, L(x) = (κ² + ω)(x − xᵘ)² + ωu²/(κ² + ω), proves global optimality and the upper-bound choice. With κ = 1/2 and ω = 1/4, L = (1/2)(x + u)² + u²/2. For u = 1, n = 0, choose x = −1, Π = 1/2, j = 1 and L = 1/2. Completely stabilizing inflation instead requires x = −2 and gives L = 1; completely stabilizing the gap gives Π = 1 and also L = 1. A nonzero cost wedge prevents both from being zero.

With u = 0 and n = −2, the loss minimum is x = Π = 0, implemented by j = −2. The earlier feedback rule delivered x = −1 because it did not directly offset the natural-rate disturbance. With n = −6, the floor prevents full stabilization: x = −4, Π = −2 and L = 8. Other instruments could change the feasible set, but that requires specifying their transmission and costs. Our one-date optimum holds terminal expectations fixed; it is not a commitment solution for the entire forward-looking path.

ExperimentMechanism made explicitWhat remains conditional
IS–LM demand or credit premiumSpending changes, money-demand feedback and expected real financing costsFixed price, given expectations, productive capacity, chosen monetary instrument and omitted future fiscal financing effects
Price-level AD–ASReal balances interact with a rising short-run price schedulePredetermined reference price and explicit supply shift; no autonomous law of persistent inflation
Finite real benchmarkTechnology changes resources and the marginal return to capitalFlexible adjustment, fixed labor, log preferences, full depreciation and no nominal or financial friction
Finite New Keynesian systemForward spending, expected inflation, cost wedges and a rate rule with a floorShock-specific natural benchmarks, supplied information and terminal conditions, local linear equations

These models organize competing interpretations; they do not identify shocks merely by naming a residual. A financial spread can move IS through z, or enter a richer dynamic demand equation as a financing wedge, but the reduced n disturbance does not by itself identify its financial origin. Policy rates often respond to worsening forecasts, so a negative correlation between rates and output is not the causal effect of a rate cut. Separating demand, supply, credit and policy requires measured quantities and prices, expectations and information dates, the operating regime, and a justified source of variation. Identification and time-series and panel methods explain why simultaneity, common shocks and measurement matter.

Finally, the flexible-price natural allocation need not be socially efficient when market power or other real wedges remain. Stabilizing x around that allocation is not automatically a complete welfare objective. The real benchmark's optimality is conditional on its own feasible set and preferences. Distribution, unemployment risk, productive government investment, international flows and financial distress may change a policy ranking. Before using a multiplier or simulated response for a decision, name the model, instrument, expectation rule, boundary condition and omitted channel that could reverse it.

Exercises

  1. A financing disturbance. In Worked example 1's baseline, raise only z from 0 to 3. Solve Y, ι, C and I at fixed m = 50, and check both markets. Find the increase in G, with T fixed, that restores baseline output under that money instrument. Separately keep G = 20 and peg ι = 3: solve output and required money. State the fiscal-financing qualification.
  2. A forbidden algebraic root. Keep Worked example 1's baseline goods schedules and nonnegative-rate restriction, but choose m = 80. Find the algebraic solution. Does replacing its rate by zero while retaining output clear both markets? If the instrument instead becomes a zero-rate peg, find output and the required m. Explain why these are different experiments.
  3. Price level versus inflation. Re-derive both positive-price equilibria in Worked example 2 and prove uniqueness on P > 0. Compute the difference between their output levels without rounding. If the preceding price is 2 and next period's price stays at the solved value, give current and next log inflation. Explain why equal inflation does not establish equal shocks.
  4. A different real investment share. In the finite real model set Y₀ = 15, A₁ = 4 and βR = 1/2. Derive and globally certify investment and both consumptions. Then double A₁ alone. Explain both the marginal-return change and the unchanged or changed current investment, and identify two assumptions behind your result.
  5. Anticipated future cost pressure. Use Worked example 4's coefficients, dates 0 and 1 and terminal x₂ = Π₂ = 0. Announce u₁ = 1 at date 0; every other n, u and v is zero. Solve the complete path and verify all three equations at date 0. Contrast date 0 with a baseline forecast of no shock followed by an unanticipated date-1 realization.
  6. A two-date floor episode. Under the same coefficients and zero terminal values, announce n₀ = n₁ = −6, with all u and v zero. Solve backward, report each requested and actual rate, and verify the binding-floor inequalities. Why is checking only the last date insufficient? Would supplying nonzero terminal forecasts necessarily give the same path?
  7. Tradeoff and feasibility. In the one-date loss problem let κ = 1/2 and ω = 1/4. First take u = 2, n = −1: find the optimum and loss, then compare complete inflation stabilization with complete gap stabilization. Separately set u = 1, n = −5 and impose j ≥ −2. Find the feasible optimum and prove it is global. Do not use the chapter's feedback rule in place of the requested optimization.
  8. Observational equivalence and the output benchmark. With Worked example 4's coefficients and zero future forecasts, only x = −1 and Π = −1/2 are observed; the rate is unobserved. Construct one explanation with v = 0 and another with n = 0, calculating u and the rate in both. Does observing x and Π identify a demand disturbance? Separately, actual output and flexible-price output both fall from 100 to 90. Compute the new natural-output gap and the gap against an unchanged reference of 100. State what extra evidence would help distinguish the two monetary explanations and why a zero natural gap need not establish social efficiency.
Complete solutions

  1. The premium lowers a from 58 to 52, so Y = (52 + 20)/(3/5) = 120 and ι = (60 − 50)/5 = 2. Consumption is 20 + (3/5)100 = 80; investment is 30 − 2(2 + 3) = 20. Goods clear as 120 = 80 + 20 + 20, and money demand is 60 − 10 = 50. To restore a = 58, increase G by bz = 6 to 26. Then Y = 130, ι = 3, C = 86 and I = 18, with 86 + 18 + 26 = 130.

    At a rate peg of 3 with G = 20, Y = (52 − 6)/(2/5) = 115, C = 77, I = 18 and m = 115/2 − 15 = 85/2. All quantities remain in their domains. Restoring output through current government borrowing has not accounted for later taxes, debt service or their effects on current behavior. These calculations compare a maintained current spending mechanism, not lifetime welfare or sustainable debt policy.

  2. At m = 80, Y = (58 + (2/5)80)/(3/5) = 150, and ι = (75 − 80)/5 = −1. This violates the rate domain. Replacing ι by zero while keeping Y = 150 gives goods expenditure 20 + (3/5)130 + 30 + 20 = 148, not 150, and money demand 75, not 80. Thus neither equation survives that clipping.

    A zero-rate peg instead implies (2/5)Y = 58, so Y = 145, C = 95 and I = 30; goods expenditure is 145. The necessary money is m = 145/2 = 72.5. This clears both markets with an endogenous quantity, but it does not implement the original fixed m = 80. Accommodating excess money at a floor would require a changed money-demand or asset-market specification, not an undocumented arithmetic repair.

  3. For the spending shift, 50P + 30 = 320/3 + 200/(3P); multiplying by 3P yields 150P² − 230P − 200 = 0. For the supply shift, 50P + 20 = 290/3 + 200/(3P) yields exactly the same equation. Its roots are (23 ± √1729)/30; since √1729 > 23, exactly one is positive. Alternatively, demand is strictly decreasing and inverse supply strictly increasing, proving at most one intersection, and the positive root establishes existence. It lies in the stated output and rate domains.

    The output difference is (50P + 30) − (50P + 20) = 10 goods per period exactly. Both give current Π = 100 ln[(23 + √1729)/60] ≈ 7.357949 points; next inflation is 100 ln(P/P) = 0. The equality of current price changes is consistent with two distinct mechanisms here. It cannot by itself identify either disturbance or establish persistent inflation.

  4. F′(I) = −1/(15 − I) + 1/(4I). The root satisfies 15 − I = 4I, hence I = 3, C₀ = 12 and C₁ = 4√3. The second derivative is strictly negative for 0 < I < 15, and utility tends to minus infinity at both endpoints. The feasible stationary point is therefore the unique global maximum.

    After A₁ doubles to 8, investment and current consumption remain 3 and 12; C₁ becomes 8√3. The marginal product doubles from 2/√3 to 4/√3, while terminal marginal utility halves. Their product, weighted by βR, is still 1/12. Log utility makes ln A₁ an additive constant; multiplicative production with full depreciation and the supplied terminal rule makes the remaining investment tradeoff unchanged. Credit limits, different preferences, labor adjustment or additional continuation value could alter this result.

  5. At date 1, x₁ = −1, Π₁ = 1/2 and j₁ = 1; the floor is slack. At date 0, X = −1, E = 1/2, B = 1/4, n₀ = v₀ = 0. Thus x₀ = [−1 + 1/2 − 2(1/4)]/2 = −1/2, Π₀ = 1/4 − 1/4 = 0 and j₀ = 0. Demand checks as −1 − (0 − 1/2) = −1/2; supply as (1/2)(1/2) + (1/2)(−1/2) = 0; policy as max{−2,2(0)} = 0. Total nominal rates are 2 and 3 at dates 0 and 1.

    The negative current gap coexists with zero current inflation because expected future inflation offsets the gap term. Under the stipulated earlier baseline forecast of no shock, date-0 x, Π and j would all be zero; the date-1 realization would then change the plan. A genuinely uncertain forecast requires its actual conditional probabilities and cannot be replaced by perfect foresight without explanation.

  6. At date 1, the unconstrained request −3 violates the floor. The correct solution is (x₁,Π₁,j₁) = (−4,−2,−2), with requested rate −4. At date 0, X = −4 and E = −2. The unconstrained formula gives x₀ᵘ = [−4 − 2 − 6 − 2(−1)]/2 = −5, Π₀ᵘ = −1 − 5/2 = −7/2 and j₀ᵘ = −7. At the floor recompute x₀ = −4 + (−2 − 6 + 2) = −10, Π₀ = −1 − 5 = −6 and j₀ = −2. Requested −12 is below −2, so the branch is consistent.

    At date 0 demand is −4 − [−2 − (−2) − (−6)] = −10. The nominal rate is zero in ordinary units, yet expected deflation makes the expected real log rate ι₀ − E₀Π₁ = 0 − (−2) = 2, above the natural real rate 2 + n₀ = −4. Future weakness and deflation enter today's equations, so checking only date 1 omits important terms. Nonzero terminal forecasts generally alter the last-date solution and transmit backward. The unique solution is conditional on that boundary, and these large gaps should not be treated as a quantitatively reliable linearized forecast.

  7. The completed square is L = (x + u)²/2 + u²/2. For u = 2, the unconstrained minimum is x = −2, Π = 1, j = n − x = 1 and L = 2. This satisfies j ≥ −2. Complete inflation stabilization requires x = −4 and j = 3, giving L = 4. Complete gap stabilization requires x = 0, j = −1 and Π = 2, again L = 4. Both alternatives are feasible; the loss weight favors the intermediate choice.

    For u = 1, n = −5, the unconstrained x = −1 requires j = −4 and is infeasible. The floor imposes x ≤ −3. Since the square (x + 1)² is minimized on that set at x = −3, choose j = −2, Π = −1/2 and L = 1/4 + 9/4 = 5/2. This is a global certificate, not only a first-order condition. The objective and feasible set, rather than the earlier feedback coefficients, determine this answer.

  8. Supply implies u = Π − x/2 = 0. With v = 0, policy gives j = 2Π = −1, above the floor. Demand x = n − j then gives n = x + j = −2. This is a natural-rate disturbance. Alternatively, impose n = 0. Demand requires j = 1, and the policy equation gives v = j − 2Π = 2. This is a policy disturbance; u remains zero. Thus the same two observations do not identify the demand explanation. Observing the nominal rate would distinguish these two stipulated cases, but extracting a structural shock still requires their expectation, natural-output, natural-rate and policy-rule assumptions.

    When Y = Yⁿ = 90, the natural-output gap is 100 ln(90/90) = 0. Against the unchanged reference it is 100 ln(90/100) ≈ −10.536052 points. One describes relative demand versus the current flexible-price benchmark; the other describes a decline from the old level. Helpful evidence includes the actual rate, dated forecasts, policy announcements or surprises, measured credit spreads and an independently justified natural-output/rate model. An identified policy surprise needs a design separating policy news from news about the economy. Zero gap need not mean social efficiency because the natural allocation can retain market-power, tax or other real distortions; neither these observations nor the gap definition supplies a full welfare criterion.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back: explain to a colleague why an output multiplier changes when the monetary instrument changes, why a price-level rise need not continue as inflation, and why the terminal condition belongs in a forward-looking model. Show one equation that must be recomputed when a rate floor binds. Contrast a technology-driven output decline with a negative gap against shock-specific natural output.

Teach-back checklist

A complete explanation names which of M and ι is fixed, traces the investment and money-demand feedback, and checks both markets. It computes inflation from two dated prices, so a permanently higher but thereafter constant price has zero subsequent inflation. Forward equations use next-date forecasts; the finite terminal values allow backward solution and are assumptions. At a floor, x = X + σ(E + n − jmin) must be recomputed before inflation and the requested-rate inequality are checked. Technology may change Yⁿ; x measures Y relative to that new benchmark, not relative to an unchanged trend. None of these mathematical statements alone identifies an observed causal shock.

Delayed check: after several days, use Worked example 1's baseline to raise G and T each by 6 at fixed m = 50. Find output and the rate. In the one-date New Keynesian system with Worked example 4's coefficients, zero future forecasts and n = −4, u = v = 0, find the equilibrium and check the floor, including equality. Explain why neither answer is an infinite-horizon determinacy result.

Delayed-check answer

The balanced-budget change raises a by 6 − (3/5)6 = 12/5, so output rises by (12/5)/(3/5) = 4 to 134. The rate becomes (67 − 50)/5 = 17/5. With T = 26, C = 424/5 and I = 116/5, resources are 134 = 424/5 + 116/5 + 26. In the dynamic system's one-date problem, x = −2, Π = −1 and j = −2; requested 2Π = −2 equals the floor. Both branch formulas coincide. The first model is static and the second uses supplied next-date forecasts; neither proves uniqueness without a terminal boundary over an infinite horizon.

Reproduce and extend

Download the synthetic announced paths, standard-library Python solver and README. The lab uses exact fractions, backward solution and explicit validation for a bounded finite system; its JSON results report requested and actual rates and equation residuals. Change the terminal values to see which predictions depend on that assumption. A separate chapter checker solves simultaneous equations under enumerated floor regimes, verifies the chapter arithmetic and tests invalid inputs and deliberately broken calculations. Agreement verifies these computations, not the empirical adequacy of the model.

Source routes are scoped to inspected primary teaching and author materials: IS–LM and instrument choice, real resource and equilibrium conditions, forward demand and inflation, and stabilization tradeoffs. Graduate microfoundations, stochastic equilibrium selection and structural estimation remain later work. Next, Fiscal policy and public debt will develop the government financing and intertemporal constraints held outside our short-run spending calculations.

Sources and further study

  • Ricardo Caballero, MIT 14.02 — Lecture 10 review transcript (Spring 2023) — Primary instructor method route for planned goods expenditure, the fixed-price output closure, interest-sensitive investment, money demand, and the distinction between a chosen money quantity and an accommodated rate peg. The chapter independently derives its own linear coefficients, feasible-domain checks and comparative statics.
  • Christian Wolf, MIT 14.05 — Lecture 15: Real Business Cycle Model (Fall 2025) — Primary instructor route for production and capital resources, household intertemporal conditions, marginal factor returns, market clearing and the need for initial/boundary conditions. The chapter's two-date fixed-labor log-utility economy and global proof are original and narrower than the full RBC model.
  • Jordi Galí — Rethinking the New Keynesian Model, Keynes Lecture, Cambridge (April 2025) — Primary author method route for the three-equation dynamic demand, forward inflation and nominal-rate structure, and the relationship of log demand equations to the Euler condition and goods-market clearing. The chapter explicitly supplies its own reduced coefficients, shock-specific gap definition, zero-inflation normalization, finite terminal conditions and floor proof.
  • Christian Wolf, MIT 14.05 — Lecture 22: Optimal Monetary Policy Design (Fall 2025) — Primary instructor method route for a quadratic inflation/activity loss, a constrained policy choice and the stabilization tradeoff introduced by a cost-push wedge. The chapter derives its own one-date completed-square certificate and rate-floor constraint, and separates the stated loss from an estimated social welfare function.
